Ribbon construction runs a BFS in the slice starting with polygons adjacent to one contour and ending with polygons adjacent to the previous contour [S1].

The claim states that ribbon construction runs a BFS in the slice starting with polygons adjacent to one contour and ending with polygons adjacent to the previous contour. This is explicitly confirmed in Source [S1] under the section 'Constructing Ribbons and Contours', which states: 'Ribbons are constructed by running a breadth-first traversal in the slice starting with the polygons adjacent to one contour and ending with the polygons adjacent to the previous contour.'

The claim states that the method builds on the concept of Reeb graphs for topology analysis. The provided evidence explicitly describes an algorithm that encodes topology in an 'augmented Reeb graph' (Section 2.1), isolates handles using this graph (Section 2.2), and defines cycles in the Reeb graph as corresponding to handles. The entire methodology described in the source is based on constructing and analyzing this graph to perform topological analysis (specifically, noise removal).

For such slices, the distance function is analyzed on a polygon-by-polygon basis using a BFS over polygons in the current slice [S1].

The claim states that for certain slices (specifically those with intraribbon handles), the distance function is analyzed on a polygon-by-polygon basis using a BFS over polygons in the current slice. The source text explicitly confirms this in the 'Traversal Revisited' section: 'For such cases, we analyze the distance function on a polygon-by-polygon basis within the relevant slice. Specifically, we use a breadth-first traversal over the polygons in the current slice...' This matches the claim exactly.

The method was introduced by Wood et al. [S1] as a way to remove excess topology from isosurfaces [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the method involves sweeping through the volume to encode topology in an augmented Reeb graph, isolating handles, measuring their size, and removing them if they are sufficiently small. The text also attributes the pseudo-code and details of the construction to 'Wood [2003]' and references 'Guskov and Wood [2001]', confirming the authorship by Wood et al. The purpose is described as removing 'topological noise (handles)' which corresponds to 'excess topology'.
supported
A contour is an oriented closed polyline formed by the intersection of the isosurface with a planar cross-section (data plane) [S1].

The source text explicitly defines a contour in Section 2.1: 'The isosurface intersects each such plane along a set of contours (oriented closed polylines)'. This matches the claim's definition of an oriented closed polyline formed by the intersection of the isosurface with a planar cross-section (data plane).
supported
If the size is sufficiently small, the handle is removed [S1].

The claim is explicitly stated in the summary of the approach within Source [S1]: '—if the size is sufficiently small, remove the handle (see Section 2.4).' Additionally, the notes list 'Step 4: If the size is sufficiently small, remove the handle.' Therefore, the evidence directly supports the claim.

The handle is isolated by performing a BFS through the graph to find the shortest graph cycle between $c_1$ and $c_2$ [S1].

The source text explicitly states in the notes and the algorithm details: 'When a Reeb cycle is detected, isolate the handle by performing a breadth-first search through the graph to find the shortest graph cycle between the two like-labeled contour nodes (e.g., c1 to c2).' This matches the claim exactly.

Detect Intraribbon Handles: Standard z-interval traversal may miss handles entirely contained within a single ribbon (slice), which occur in 1–10% of slices [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that 'when a handle is entirely contained within a ribbon, (i.e., within a slice of the volume), it is not initially detected during the traversal' and that 'In practice, these intraribbon handles occur for 1–10% of the slices of a volume.' It further details the method to detect them by computing the Euler characteristic.

The Reeb cycle path consists of alternating ribbon and contour nodes and defines the handle [S1].

The source text explicitly states in the section '2.2 Isolating Handles Using the Augmented Reeb Graph' under the subsection 'Finding Cycles in the Reeb graph' (specifically in the provided notes/pseudo-code description): 'The Reeb cycle path consists of alternating ribbon and contour nodes and defines the handle.' This matches the claim exactly.

Memory complexity supports out-of-core processing due to ordered traversal through slices, keeping surface access local [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the method uses an 'ordered traversal through the slices' which 'allows for the out-of-core processing of the volume data.' It contrasts this with polygon-by-polygon traversal which requires 'highly irregular data access.' Furthermore, regarding intraribbon handles, the text notes that 'confining the per-voxel traversal to the slice keeps our surface access local, allowing our method to support out-of-core processing.' Thus, the claim that memory complexity supports out-of-core processing due to ordered traversal through slices, keeping surface access local, is fully supported by the text.
supported
Limitations include not being guaranteed to find globally minimum cuts due to local search only [S1].

The claim states that limitations include not being guaranteed to find globally minimum cuts due to local search only. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'We search for nonseparating cuts only in a local region, one handle at a time. While we are not guaranteed to find the globally minimum cuts, our algorithm can operate out-of-core and generate fast approximations.' This directly supports every part of the claim.

Sweep and Encode Topology: Sweep through the volume along parallel data planes (z-intervals) [S1].

The claim states that the method involves sweeping through the volume along parallel data planes (z-intervals) to encode topology. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the algorithm summary ('sweep through the volume to encode the topology in an augmented Reeb graph') and in Section 2.1 ('Our approach uses an axis-aligned sweep through the volume which visits the grid data along parallel data planes... We therefore analyze the boundary at discrete z intervals'). The evidence directly supports every part of the claim.

The claim states that 'Time complexity is not given in the sources [S1].' However, the provided evidence from Source [S1] explicitly discusses performance characteristics and efficiency, such as 'fast approximations,' 'out-of-core processing,' 'less dense Reeb graph,' and comparisons to other methods like 'Cut Graphs' which 'analyze the entire surface.' While it does not provide a formal Big-O notation (e.g., O(n log n)), it provides qualitative evidence regarding the algorithm's efficiency and complexity relative to other methods. Therefore, the claim that time complexity is 'not given' is factually incorrect because performance/complexity characteristics are discussed.
